newsitem.title: BERMUDA: Few nations seen benefiting from debt relief.
newsitem.headline: Few nations seen benefiting from debt relief.

text.p: Proposals to bail out countries pushed by almost unpayable debts into deepening poverty are so rigid that very few stand much hope of help before the turn of the century, the Commonwealth said.

In a confidential report, obtained by Reuters on Tuesday and on the top of the agenda at this week's meeting of Commonwealth finance ministers in this Caribbean island, the group argues that the international community have imposed too many rules.
"These restrictions reduce to only 11 the number of countries likely to receive multilateral debt relief, and delay relief so that only three will receive comprehensive treatment," it said.

Several of the 53 members of the Commonwealth, which groups memebrs of the former British Empire, are saddled with large debts to multilateral financial institutions such as the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank.
Historically, the poorer countries have been forced to borrow from these institutions, whose industrial nation shareholders only recently agreed to even consider writing off some of the debt.
By contrast, major developing countries such as in Latin America were able to borrow from commercial banks with whom they subsequently rescheduled defaulted debt payments into far easier terms.
Britain has been pressing for greater help, including selling some of the IMF's $40 billion in gold reserves, to release funds for the heavily indebted poor countries.
The issue will be one of the main topics at next week's annual IMF/World Bank meeting in Washington when industrial countries will come under further pressure to do more to help the poor.
"In theory up to 20 countries are eligible (for debt relief). But, in reality they are focusing on only two or three," one Commonwealth official said.

"The proposals currently being developed need considerable strengthening if they are to have a decisive impact on the multilateral debt problems of heavily indebted poor countries" the report said, adding that it welcomed steps taken thus far.
The report, which Commonwealth sources said had input from the British Treasury, said the criteria and time-frame for countries to join in any relief scheme were too restrictive.

For example, a country has to have a proven three-year economic track record before individual creditor countries will help and another three after that before the multilateral financial agencies step in.
The question of the IMF selling some of its gold has yet to be resolved after two years of debate, with countries such as Germany fiercely opposed to selling what they see as the IMF's family jewels.
Last week, the IMF's board put off any decision on the sale of gold until consensus could be reached.
Financing the relief is also open to doubt.
The report said that the IMF and World Bank estimate the cost of the initiative would be $5.6 billion, of which they will only provide $2 billion.

It urged that the criteria be changed so that as many countries as possible get relief by 2000 and that it is funded fairly among all the creditors and not shouldered by budget- conscious industrial countries.
